messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Non-profit Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajesh was sixty-eight years old, a divorced man who had spent the last two decades working at a small nonprofit that supported immigrant families. He was known there as quiet, meticulous, and unfailingly reliable—a colleague who never missed a deadline, but who always positioned himself at the far end of the conference table, his back to the wall, eyes scanning the room as though he were waiting for something to go wrong. What his coworkers did not know was that Rajesh had not slept through the night in over two years, that he had learned to flinch before anyone touched him, and that sometimes, when the memories came, he would excuse himself to the bathroom and press his fingernails into his forearm until the pain drowned out the sounds he heard in his head.

The event that had set all of this in motion had happened late one evening after a community fundraiser. Rajesh had stayed behind to lock up, and a man he vaguely recognized from a previous event had followed him inside. What happened next was over in minutes, but for Rajesh it had never ended. He could still feel the pressure of the man’s hand over his mouth, the weight pinning him to the cold floor. He could still hear the low, deliberate breathing that had been the only sound besides the hum of the fluorescent lights. In the months that followed, he told no one. He told himself that he was a grown man, that he should have fought harder, that his reactions since then just proved what a lousy coper he really was. He began to believe that he would never feel normal emotions again—that the part of him that had once laughed easily and trusted people had been permanently erased. He had become an outsider, even in his own life.

The symptoms arrived slowly and then all at once. At first it was just a heightened alertness: he would listen for footsteps in the hallway of his apartment building, his heart pounding at the sound of a door opening. Soon he could not bear to be alone in a room. He started taking his work breaks in the communal kitchen, making small talk he did not want just to have someone nearby. At home he left the television on all night, not for company but to mask the ambient sounds that might signal someone entering. A sudden loud noise—a car backfiring, a dropped tray in the cafeteria—would send him into a state of rigid vigilance. The worst was unexpected touch. When a colleague placed a hand on his shoulder to get his attention, Rajesh would jerk away, his breath catching, his mind flashing to that cold floor before he could stop it. He began to sit with his back to the wall at every meal, every meeting, positioning himself so that he could see the entire room. His coworkers noticed; they stopped touching him.

The memories themselves were not just visual. When they returned, often without warning, Rajesh would hear the same low breathing, as though it were happening in the room with him. He would feel a sharp pain in his ribs, in his jaw, exactly where the man had pressed him down. And when he tried to describe any of this—to his doctor, to the therapist he finally saw once—the words would not come. He knew what had happened, could replay it in perfect detail, but his mouth would go dry and the sentences would dissolve. He felt trapped inside his own mind.

The self-harm began about a year in. After a particularly vivid memory that left him shaking and nauseous, Rajesh found himself digging his fingernails into his forearm so hard that the crescents of blood surprised him. The sharp sting brought a kind of relief, a way to externalize the chaos that lived inside him. He started doing it more often—a small cut with a kitchen knife, a burn from a lighter—always in private, always when the feelings threatened to overwhelm him. He told himself it was the only thing that still felt real.

He came to therapy because his supervisor, concerned after seeing the scars on his wrist during a hand-delivery of paperwork, had gently insisted. Rajesh knew he could not keep living like this, but what he feared most was that he was right—that his emotions were permanently broken, that he would always be an outsider, that no amount of talking could change what he had become. Still, he sat down in the office, his back to the wall, and tried to find the words.
